report:
**Conclusion:** Contrary to your initial thought, clinical evidence demonstrates that **yes, denosumab (Prolia) significantly reduces the risk of vertebral fractures** during ongoing treatment. 

### Key Evidence

1. **Efficacy During Active Treatment**  
   In the landmark Phase 3 FREEDOM trial, postmenopausal women with osteoporosis receiving denosumab every 6 months achieved a **68% relative reduction in new vertebral fractures** over three years compared to placebo (2.3% vs. 7.2%, *p* < 0.001) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). Systematic reviews and network meta-analyses confirm that denosumab provides substantial protection against vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fractures (https://www.bmj.com/content/381/bmj-2021-068033).

2. **Why Misconceptions Exist: The Discontinuation Rebound**  
   Your impression may arise from research on what happens when treatment stops. Denosumab reversibly inhibits RANKL (a key signaling protein for osteoclasts). Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab does not incorporate into bone tissue. Consequently, stopping denosumab without transitioning to an alternative antiresorptive agent (such as a bisphosphonate) causes a rapid "rebound" surge in bone turnover, rapid loss of bone mineral density, and an elevated risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3617467/, https://academic.oup.com/jbmr/article/37/11/2112/7512382).

**Summary:** Denosumab strongly prevents vertebral fractures while therapy is continuously maintained. However, stopping treatment abruptly without sequential therapy creates a rebound fracture risk.
